prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states there, opening the field of moire quantum materials

statement.case_for: Four of eight openings, including mine, placed B033 first, and I do not take that as merit in itself. The merit is that the discovery rests on a single, analysable mechanism. Bistritzer and MacDonald showed in a continuum model that interlayer tunnelling in a small-angle bilayer renormalises the Dirac velocity to zero near a magic angle. This is a controlled, almost textbook perturbative argument, and it was written down years before anyone could build the device. Jarillo-Herrero's group then showed that the predicted flat bands are electrically tunable and host correlated insulators and superconductivity, and the result was reproduced widely. That sequence of a clean model, a sharp experimental test and a new tunable platform is the pattern I trust most. The twist angle is a control knob for the ratio of interaction to bandwidth, so one can study strongly correlated electrons in a way that was previously impossible. A theory-plus-experiment prize with three names fits the attribution well.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the microscopic origin of the superconductivity is still unsettled, so the prize would honour a platform and a phase diagram rather than an understood mechanism, which is a criterion I normally care about. Credit is also uncomfortable: Eva Y. Andrei's earlier STM evidence of flat-band physics in twisted layers, and the parallel Dean and Kim device work, are not fully reflected in a Jarillo-Herrero, MacDonald, Bistritzer trio, and the shortlist lists four credited names for a three-person limit. Finally, the field is only about seven years old as an experimental programme, and the Committee could reasonably want more time to see which results survive sample-to-sample variation.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks (B026) first as a patient measurement advance: magic-wavelength trapping, 1e-18 uncertainty, and a coming redefinition of the second, with Katori and Ye as a compact, defensible pair, and he places twisted graphene only third.
responses.response: I agree that B026 is the cleanest attribution on the list and that its maturity is unquestionable, and I keep it as an alternative. Where I differ is on how much weight the practical readiness of a redefinition should carry. A prize is for the discovery, and the discovery here is an elegant and already recognised extension of precision spectroscopy, whereas moire flat bands opened a new regime of physics that could not be reached before. I also note the irony that the magic-angle idea in graphene and the magic-wavelength idea in clocks are both cancellation arguments, and I find the former the more surprising. If the Committee prefers a measurement-centred prize, I would not object, but I do not think B026 should displace B033.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B010) first and B033 only fifth, partly because a prize so soon after the 2025 superconducting-circuit award may be too close in subject, and because the credited Blais, Wallraff, Schoelkopf names leave out co-authors of the 2004 proposal.
responses.response: The proximity argument is fair and it is the reason I did not rank B010 higher. If 2025 has just honoured macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits, then circuit QED reads as the next chapter of one story. Twisted graphene is a different community, a different problem (strong correlations) and a different set of tools. I would ask Johansson to say whether he sees circuit QED as a separate achievement in conceptual terms, or mainly as a platform success. For me, the novelty of the idea (a flat-band mechanism with a sharp analytic prediction) is greater for B033.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B033 only fourth and cautions that recognition may be somewhat early, since sample dependence is a concern and the pairing mechanism is open, while placing optical lattices and clocks above it.
responses.response: I take the sample-dependence point seriously and I agree the pairing mechanism is open. But the discovery claimed is the existence of the correlated insulating and superconducting states and their tunability, not a theory of the pairing. That has been reproduced by many independent groups, and by now across graphene multilayers and other moire materials, so it is not fragile. On B037 specifically, I see it as a Hubbard-model simulator whose main discoveries are of the Mott transition and later microscopy, and with five credited names it is harder to carve cleanly than B033.

responses.point: Eriksson also puts B033 first but proposes Andrei as the third laureate, in place of Bistritzer, arguing that Andrei's STM work on flat bands and Van Hove singularities is an early experimental strand.
responses.response: I understand the instinct and I do not think it is wrong on the merits, but I would still pick Bistritzer. The distinguishing feature of this prize is that the flat-band mechanism was predicted analytically, and the Bistritzer-MacDonald paper is that prediction; removing one of its two authors would blur the one-two punch of theory and experiment. Andrei's work is real and earlier on the experimental side, but it showed signatures of electronic localisation and Van Hove singularities rather than the correlated and superconducting phases that define the discovery. I would rather admit the attribution is imperfect than distort the logic of the citation.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee gives Andrei, rather than Bistritzer, the third seat, and how priority between her STM work and the 2018 transport results is weighed.
How much the unresolved pairing mechanism should count against a prize this soon, given reproducibility across many labs.
My knowledge of who measured what first is from memory and is not independently checked.
Whether B009 (topological insulators) is a stronger fit once the missing theory credits (Mele, Bernevig, Zhang) are weighed; I am not confident in my own judgement there.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. I have no known collaboration with any credited candidate. I note only that I am in the same Gothenburg physics environment as Goran Johansson and Eva Olsson (Chalmers), which is not a connection to any shortlisted candidate.
